svg.title: Layers and attention heads
svg.text: 4 · Every layer has twelve heads, each reading the sentence differently
Left: two single heads, and how one word divides its attention across the sentence — those bars sum to 1.
reads the word immediately before — every time
reaches across the sentence to a related word
one square per head. darker = it ignores
the words and parks on punctuation.
weights and do not sum to 1.
Heads specialise, but most of them are not doing anything tidy.
Counting only what the real words point at: 57 of the 144 send over 70% of their attention to punctuation and the
sentence markers — a known idling behaviour — and 23 mostly read the words.
Within one layer a head is a 64-number slice of the 768 — twelve slices attending independently, then joined back together: 12 × 64 = 768.
A layer is one round of that, and the twelve layers do not share heads — each has its own twelve, hence 144 in total. Stacking them lets a
token be influenced by a word it never looked at directly, reached through whatever the layer below folded in.
